IB Computer Science

A4.1 Machine Learning Fundamentals

Topic A4: Machine Learning | Patterns, Predictions & Decisions

The Big Question

🤔 If an AI writes an essay…

does it understand what it wrote?

❌ Common misconception: “Machine learning thinks like a human.”

It doesn’t “know” meanings the way humans do.

✅ Reality: ML systems learn patterns in data and produce outputs that look intelligent.

That makes data quality and evaluation essential.

AI vs ML vs deep learning

How are these terms related?

AI is the big umbrella.

Machine learning is a way to build AI using data.

Deep learning is ML using neural networks with multiple layers.

Common mistake

Deep learning is a subset of machine learning — not a separate field.

Types of machine learning

What changes when the data has “answers” vs no answers?

Supervised learning — labelled data

Unsupervised learning — no labels

Reinforcement learning — rewards from interaction

Transfer learning — reuse a trained model

Typical outputs

Regression: number (e.g., house price)

Classification: category (e.g., spam/not spam)

Clustering: groups (e.g., customer segments)

Supervised learning: two common tasks

Are you predicting a number or choosing a category?

Regression

Predicts a value on a range (e.g., temperature, exam score).

Classification

Chooses one label from a set (e.g., fraud/legit).

Exam tip: if the output is continuous → regression. If it’s one of discrete options → classification.

Where ML shows up in the real world

Which problems are easiest for machines to learn from data?

Recommendations: Netflix/Spotify suggestions

Vision: recognizing objects in images

Language: translation and chatbots

Forecasting: demand, prices, traffic

Generative AI

Generative AI creates new content, but still learns patterns from training data.

That makes evaluation and ethics central (see A4.4).

🧠 Quick Check

Classify each scenario by learning type.

A. Predicting house prices from size and location

B. Grouping customers into “similar” segments without labels

C. An AI learns to play a game using rewards for winning

A: supervised regression

B: unsupervised clustering

C: reinforcement learning

Training vs inference

Why does training often need more hardware than using the model?

Training updates model weights repeatedly (lots of computation).

Inference uses the trained model to make predictions (often cheaper per request).

Both depend on data movement: RAM/VRAM, storage, and network bandwidth.

Key requirement

Many ML computations are matrix operations → benefit from parallel hardware.

Hardware for machine learning

What hardware choices change speed, cost, and privacy?

GPU accelerates parallel calculations (training and some inference).

TPU is specialized ML hardware (often cloud).

NPU supports on-device ML (lower latency, often more private).

Deployment platforms

Laptop: small models + experimentation

Workstation: dedicated GPU for bigger training

Edge: low latency + privacy, limited power

Cloud/HPC: scalable compute, ongoing cost + data transfer

🧠 Quick Check

A university wants to analyse live video lectures to generate real-time captions.

Recommend two hardware/platform choices and justify them briefly.

Option 1: cloud GPUs/TPUs — high throughput for video workloads, scalable.

Option 2: edge device with NPU/GPU — lower latency and improved privacy (but limited power).

Misconception Check

True or False: “More compute always beats better data.”

False. Poor-quality data can produce poor models no matter how powerful the hardware is.

That’s why data preprocessing (A4.2 HL) is often a huge part of real ML work.

Key Takeaways

  • ML is a subset of AI that learns patterns from data to make predictions.
  • Key types: supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, plus deep/transfer learning.
  • Supervised tasks include regression (numbers) and classification (categories).
  • Hardware decisions (GPU/TPU/NPU) affect speed, cost, latency, and privacy.
